analysis.one_liner: Forces any bank too big to fail — over 3% of GDP in exposure — to break up.
analysis.headline: Senator Sanders's bill to break up the largest banks was introduced in October 2018, drew zero cosponsors, was sent to the Senate Banking Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Federal Reserve to break apart any financial institution whose total exposure to the financial system equals or exceeds 3% of annual U.S. GDP — a size threshold that today's largest banks exceed. Institutions that stayed too big would be locked out of Federal Reserve emergency lending, and their insured deposits could no longer be used to fund derivatives trading or other speculative activities. The bill was read twice, referred to the Banking Committee, and received no further action. [S2] [S3] [S5]
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers. The bill attacks 'too big to fail': when a bank is so large that its collapse would wreck the financial system, the government effectively must rescue it, and the cost of that implicit guarantee lands on taxpayers and the banking public. By capping bank size at roughly 3% of GDP, cutting off Fed emergency credit for oversized institutions, and barring them from gambling with federally insured deposits, the bill would make any future bailout smaller or unnecessary. Smaller banks and credit unions would also compete against less gigantic rivals. [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Federal Reserve to require any institution whose total exposure equals or exceeds 3% of annual U.S. GDP to restructure itself down to size, with supervision by the Fed's Vice Chair for Supervision.

Cuts off any designated 'Too Big to Exist' institution from the Federal Reserve discount window, credit facilities, and other emergency support, removing the safety net that encourages giant banks to take bigger risks.

Bars institutions designated as too big from using federally insured deposits to fund speculative derivatives trading, collateralized debt obligations, and other activities that put the Deposit Insurance Fund at risk of loss.
Requires annual public testimony and reports to the House and Senate banking committees on which institutions were designated and how their restructuring is going.

analysis.who_pays: The largest Wall Street banks, which would have to split themselves into smaller firms within two years. Their shareholders would bear the disruption, and the biggest institutions would lose the competitive advantages of scale, access to Fed liquidity, and the implicit government backstop that lowers their borrowing costs. Some large corporate clients could face higher costs if they lose the ability to get all their financing from a single giant bank. [S3]

drawbacks.text: Forcing breakup on a two-year clock carries real transition risk: unwinding trillions in derivatives contracts, loans, and deposits could disrupt markets in the process, and critics argue that size alone is a blunt measure of risk rather than a precise one.

The bill excludes designated institutions from every Federal Reserve credit facility, including the discount window, which in a genuine crisis could make even a shrinking giant bank more fragile and could worsen a panic rather than contain it.
The 3%-of-GDP threshold is set by formula with no flexibility for regulators to adjust it, so a fast-growing bank could trip the limit regardless of its actual risk profile.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — that no private bank should be so large that its failure forces a public rescue — addresses a real and costly problem that ordinary taxpayers and depositors ultimately pay for. The costs fall on the banks themselves and on large corporate clients, while the main risks are execution ones: a rushed breakup or a crisis that hits before restructuring is complete. The bill is blunt but the direction is toward reducing the public's exposure to Wall Street failures.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on October 3, 2018, read twice, and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which took no action on it before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Bernie Sanders (I-VT) introduced the bill on October 3, 2018; it received no cosponsors from either party.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day it was introduced, and that is the last action ever taken on it.
The committee held no hearing, took no vote, and never reported the bill out, so the full Senate never considered it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest Wall Street banks, which kept their size, their access to Federal Reserve emergency lending, and their ability to fund trading with insured deposits. Taxpayers and depositors gained nothing from a bill that never moved.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap bank size at 3% of GDP and force the largest institutions to restructure.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred to the committee; it received no action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes were ever held, and with zero cosponsors from either party there is no record of partisan support for or against the bill; it was introduced by an independent senator and died without any recorded opposition or backing. [S4] [S5]

industries.note: The bill would force any institution with exposure of 3% of GDP or more to restructure within two years, cutting the largest banks down to size. The industry's interest in staying enormous runs against the public's interest in never again having to absorb the cost of a failing giant. [S3]

industries.industry: Wall Street derivatives and structured-finance traders
industries.note: Designated institutions could no longer use insured deposits to fund speculative derivatives, CDOs, CLOs, and structured products, which would shrink a profitable trading business. This trading activity was central to the losses that triggered public bailouts in 2008. [S3]

Breaking up the giants would reduce competition from institutions that enjoy scale advantages and an implicit government backstop. Smaller institutions' fortunes rise alongside customers who benefit from a more competitive, less systemically risky banking system. [S3]
